content:
Week 1 proved the repo could carry more than a PDF résumé. This is the refonte log: same Hugo root, different product — Paper instead of HBTheme, EN/FR pairs, typed posts, a projects catalog, and MCP when a diagram or draft needs to land in git faster. Sequel to Create a portfolio with Hugo (week 1). Version française.
From HBTheme to Paper HBTheme got the site online. Opinionated modules and an npm asset path were fine for week one; they fought custom layouts later.
The blog now runs on Paper with project overrides: bilingual header and language switcher, dark mode, menus in hugo.toml, strings in i18n. The static HTML résumés stay at the site root (index-en.html / index-fr.html); the Hugo tree is the editorial shell, not a second CV renderer.
Lesson that stuck: pick a thin theme and own the partials you care about, instead of peeling a batteries-included stack for years.
Bilingual posts as the default Every public article is a pair:
hugo/content/posts/<slug>/index.md hugo/content/posts/<slug>/index.fr.md Same translationKey, same date, same post_kind. English links French near the top (and the reverse). That discipline beats a late “we should translate the blog” rewrite.
post_kind and the projects catalog List and search templates group content by kind — article, conference, tutorial — instead of one flat chronological dump. Conference posts get a distinct treatment (kicker, featured image from the page bundle); project work lives under projects/ with repository notes so a repo can have a stable local write-up without stuffing everything into /posts.
The site stopped being “a theme with posts” and became a small content model: posts for narrative, projects for inventory, kinds for how cards and singles render.
What the stack looks like now Source of truth is still Markdown in git. The shape around it changed — static PNG below (light-theme capture; live Mermaid contrast is weak in dark mode). Source: site-refonte-flow.mmd.
MCP as the faster editorial loop Week 1 embeds were iframes and link-outs. Diagrams for systems and pipelines now start in chat: uml-mcp turns Mermaid (or other Kroki-backed types) into something you save beside the post — .mmd in the page bundle, often with an SVG — then Hugo (or the Mermaid fence) shows it.
That is the improvement that matters for shipping posts: less copy-paste from a plugin playground, more “agent writes the diagram source into the repo.” When the live renderer fights dark mode, I keep the .mmd and ship a light-theme PNG in the page bundle (this post’s stack diagram). Cursor agents also draft and edit bilingual Markdown against the same tree, so the portfolio stays reviewable diffs instead of a CMS draft queue.
I still treat agent output as a first draft. The publish bar is the same as week 1: readable English and French, working links, diagrams that match the text.
What did not change Still true Why Repo as source of truth Markdown in, HTML out Static hosting Cheap, fast, no admin to patch Substack optional Longform / email when needed; Hugo remains the professional home Iframes sparingly Demos and guest embeds — not the core content model JSON Resume and the HTML CV sit next to this shell; see professional résumé + JSON Resume.
Related posts Create a portfolio with Hugo (week 1) — HBTheme, Substack split, iframe shortcode uml-mcp — diagrams from chat via MCP — the diagram tooling this loop uses Software engineering journey — career context the portfolio supports
summary: Hugo portfolio refonte after week 1 — Paper theme, bilingual posts, post_kind and projects catalog, then MCP as the faster editorial loop.

content:
AINewsTracker turns financial news into records that can be searched, analysed and compared with market data. Version française
The project is a FastAPI service with separate routes for news, articles, companies, users, data seeding and trading strategies. Routes receive HTTP requests; services and repositories handle analysis and storage.
From a feed to an article The main path begins in app/routers/news.py. A news route dispatches work to app/core/services/news.py, which retrieves feed content and builds article records. Text analysis lives in app/core/services/metrics.py; the article repository then writes the result to MongoDB.
flowchart LR User["API client"] --> API["FastAPI<br/>app/main.py"] API --> Routes["News routes<br/>app/routers/news.py"] Routes --> Fetcher["News service<br/>app/core/services/news.py"] Sources["Financial news sources"] --> Fetcher Fetcher --> Metrics["Text metrics<br/>app/core/services/metrics.py"] Fetcher --> Repo["Article repository<br/>app/core/repo/article.py"] Repo --> Mongo[("MongoDB")] Routes describe the API surface, models define stored data, services perform the news work, and repositories isolate database access. app/main.py also configures Redis caching.
Analysis and backtesting The project documentation describes sentiment analysis, topic classification, ticker allocation and article summarisation. The strategy route sends backtest requests to app/core/trading/strategy.py.
These labels are inputs to an experiment. They do not prove that a news item caused a market move, and a historical backtest does not guarantee future performance.
API surface The published documentation covers news ingestion from RSS, GNews and named feeds; article storage and score lookup; company records and ticker lookup; and strategy execution for one or more companies. FastAPI exposes interactive documentation at /api/v1/docs on the documented local port 8000.
Running it locally cp .env.example .env pip install poetry poetry shell poetry install poetry run pytest poetry run uvicorn app.main:app --reload Docker Compose provides another entry point:
docker-compose up --build Read the architecture The complete GitDiagram includes route registrations, models, repositories, seeders, MongoDB, Redis and the trading branch. Each node links to its source file.
Interactive GitDiagram AINewsTracker project reference Source repository Published documentation The repository remains the source of truth for configuration, current endpoints and setup requirements.

The useful boundary in IPC Toolkit is clear: it provides contact routines, while the calling simulation owns time stepping and solving. Version française.
The toolkit includes barrier functions and derivatives, adaptive barrier stiffness, broad- and narrow-phase continuous collision detection, distance derivatives for edges and triangles, distance barrier potentials, and smooth or lagged dissipative friction potentials.
That list also describes the limit. IPC Toolkit is not a complete physics engine and does not include a simulation loop or solver. The upstream project points to PolyFEM and Rigid IPC as full simulation implementations that use it.
My project note keeps the repository overview with the other project documentation. The upstream README and contributor fork are the references for build details and current changes.
summary: IPC Toolkit provides reusable collision, CCD, distance and friction routines without owning the simulation loop.
title: IPC Toolkit: the contact library behind a simulation

TrueMapData starts with a measured height map and keeps the path to a useful output visible. Version française.
The project reads TrueMap v6-style and legacy files, plus GelSight-compatible layouts. Its tmd-process CLI and Python package cover filters, transforms, normal and displacement maps, defect detection, sequence export, compression and mesh formats.
The same repository reaches into surface analysis. Optional Surfalize support covers ISO 25178 roughness, while tribology and wear commands work with aligned captures, contact-style curves, wear volume series, scratches and debris-oriented maps. Mesh export can apply height-derived textures to a template using capture metadata.
That combination is useful across two neighbouring workflows: measured surfaces can feed metrology questions, or become visual assets for a graphics pipeline. The TrueMapData project note links the repository and documentation.
TrueMapData repository Documentation
summary: TrueMapData connects TrueMap and GelSight files to visualisation, surface metrics, wear analysis and mesh export.

Components22Connections17Links supported by code or README16/17 Text version of the diagram Application or demo → mathlib data and transformsmathlib data and transforms → Scene hierarchy and cameraScene hierarchy and camera → wgpu resources and passeswgpu resources and passes → Native window or web canvas The application supplies geometry and transforms. The scene layer organizes entities and cameras; the rendering layer prepares the GPU work for a native window or web canvas. This is the rendering path, not a claim that every numerical operation runs on the GPU.
Open the component-by-component code walkthrough.
Start with the storage mathlib/src/lib.rs exports dense storage alongside sparse formats such as CRS and CCS. The public API also includes matrix and vector types, matrix views and submatrices. Those choices matter before a renderer draws anything: they determine how a caller represents and passes its data.
The same entry point exposes LU, Cholesky and SVD decompositions, plus root finding and numerical integration. Optional GPU functionality sits behind a feature flag. The presence of an executor abstraction is a design choice, not a measured speedup; I have not included performance comparisons here.
Follow a transform into the scene render/src/lib.rs describes a wgpu renderer that uses mathlib for CPU transforms and camera mathematics. Its exports include World, EntityId, Transform, cameras and render targets.
The scene represents parent-child relationships with a tree. A local transform therefore belongs to a hierarchy: moving a parent changes the context in which its children are rendered. Serialization is optional and enabled through the serde feature.
The platform layer supports native windows and WebAssembly canvas targets. Keeping platform code apart from scene and numerical code gives those targets shared building blocks, although it does not prove identical behavior on every GPU or browser.
Read the workspace, not only the README The root Cargo.toml lists crates for rendering, geometry, collision, kinematics, physics, networking, parsing and neural work alongside mathlib. The README still focuses on the mathematics crate. I use the manifest and module entry points to understand the current structure.
This is exploratory code. Performance comparisons would need a reproducible benchmark with its input size and target hardware.
The heightmap above comes from mathlib/waves_heightmap.png. Browse Dimension on GitHub.
summary: Inside my Dimension workspace: matrix storage, numerical methods, scene transforms and a wgpu renderer for native and web targets.
title: Dimension: connecting Rust mathematics to a renderer

Vue calls Rocket endpoints for persistence, tenant checks and Docker actions; PostgreSQL stores workspace data and a separate adapter talks to Docker.
Components24Connections29Links supported by code or README26/29 Text version of the diagram Vue workspace UI → Rocket handlersRocket handlers → Diesel and PostgreSQLRocket handlers → Shiplift adapterShiplift adapter → Docker daemon Saving a layout goes through workspace handlers and database records. Restarting a container goes through the Shiplift adapter to Docker. PostgreSQL does not execute the Docker action, and an applet is not itself a running container. Keeping those paths separate helps explain both permissions and failure states.
Follow the handlers and Docker boundary in the architecture note.
A workspace has an owner The frontend uses Vue, while the backend uses Rust, Rocket and Diesel. In src/workspaces/handler.rs, the list handler reads the tenant identifier from a token. The handler that returns applets checks the workspace’s tenant before returning its contents.
The create-with-applets route also derives the tenant identifier from the token. That is the intended ownership model: a saved layout belongs to a user, and applets belong to a workspace.
The file contains older create and delete paths with different checks. Their presence is a reason to inspect authorization across every operation before using this as a shared service. This article describes an experiment, not a security review of a deployed system.
Docker is a separate boundary src/containers/docker.rs wraps Shiplift calls for listing containers and images, pulling images, creating containers, and stopping or restarting them. This separates the dashboard’s workspace model from Docker operations.
It also exposes a UI problem: the list helpers return an empty vector after a Docker error. An empty dashboard could therefore mean either “nothing is running” or “the service could not be reached.” I would make those states visibly different in a new version.
What the browser can embed The README records iframe login failures. Applications can restrict embedding, and authentication inside a frame may behave differently from an ordinary tab. A dashboard needs an external link for those services even when an iframe works for others.
This is an older project. The repository’s screenshot and optional GIF preserve the interface as it was; they do not demonstrate compatibility with current dependencies.
Play the original demo GIF Browse the source and original README. Both illustrations come from its images directory.
summary: A look back at DasherControl: Vue applets, Rust and Rocket handlers, persisted workspaces and a Docker interface.

Artists configure a connection, browse or search bucket files, transfer Blender dependencies, and load supported assets into the scene through operators concentrated in the add-on module.
Components12Connections19Links supported by code or README19/19 Text version of the diagram Blender panel → Active connectionActive connection → S3 or MinIO APIS3 or MinIO API → Object keys and folder treeObject keys and folder tree → Blender panelS3 or MinIO API → Temporary fileTemporary file → Blender importer Listing creates the panel’s folder view; loading an asset downloads its bytes and invokes a local importer. A listing refresh can therefore succeed while an import fails on an unsupported format. The background refresh hands UI updates back through Blender timers instead of treating the storage request as a UI operation.
Read the architecture note with the connection and import boundaries.
Make the connection explicit addon.py defines a CloudConnection property group with a provider, endpoint, bucket and region. Preferences hold multiple connections and an active connection index. The client setup chooses the S3 or MinIO path from that selection.
This is the part that interests me as both graphics and platform work: the artist works inside Blender, while the add-on translates those actions into object-storage operations.
Turn object names into folders Object storage uses keys. The refresh operator splits those keys on / and builds a nested dictionary for the panel. Folder expansion is tracked separately, so the UI can browse a hierarchy without pretending it is a local filesystem.
CloudSearchManager adds fuzzy matching with RapidFuzz. It scores filenames and path segments, gives direct substring matches priority and supports filters for scenes, meshes, images and materials.
Downloading and importing are different actions The download helper saves an object to a temporary local path. The load operator then selects a Blender importer for STL, OBJ, PLY or USD variants. Other extensions are rejected with a message. A successful transfer alone does not mean Blender has imported a usable object.
The upload-current-file operator sends the saved .blend file. Although the README discusses dependencies, I would verify texture packaging and relative paths before relying on this path to move a complete scene.
Keep the fork’s scope visible The public upstream comparison showed 10 commits ahead and 5 behind on October 23, 2026. The changed files include the add-on, packaging metadata and README. That describes repository history; it does not establish that upstream accepted those changes.
The source also uses a single S3 list_objects_v2 request, so buckets beyond one response need pagination work. These are the kinds of small workflow boundaries I want to keep visible when revisiting the project.
summary: A code tour of my Blender cloud-storage fork: multiple connections, folder browsing, fuzzy search and mesh imports.

content:
My reverse-proxy project uses Caddy on a DigitalOcean VPS, with Cloudflare DNS. Terraform creates the infrastructure, Ansible configures it, and separate checks examine the resulting service.
This article describes the repository as reviewed on October 22, 2026. The source is private, so the diagram is deliberately simplified and contains no real domains, addresses or credentials. I reviewed the code without running a deployment.
Two kinds of change Terraform manages the infrastructure layer. The DNS configuration defines apex and wildcard records, including IPv6 variants. Ansible handles the server and application configuration. A justfile provides entry points for provisioning, deployment and validation.
flowchart TD A[Local task runner or CI] --> T[Terraform] T --> V[DigitalOcean VPS] T --> D[Cloudflare DNS records] V --> N[Ansible configuration] N --> C[Caddy container] C --> S[Upstream applications] N --> B[Configuration backup] N --> Q[Configuration validation] Q --> H[Deployment diagnostics] The arrows describe responsibilities, not a guarantee that every command follows the same path. The important boundary is ownership: DNS changes should not be independently managed by two automation systems.
Read the deployment order The Caddy role starts with backup tasks, optionally prepares a CrowdSec bouncer, sets up the container, and then includes configuration-validation tasks. Those tasks check endpoint structure and TLS-provider references. For example, an endpoint needs a hostname and an upstream, redirect or wildcard configuration.
That catches a different class of problem from an HTTP probe. A configuration can be structurally valid while its upstream application is unavailable. Conversely, an existing service can still answer requests while a proposed configuration is invalid.
The repository also contains roles for Umami analytics, WireGuard and system setup. Their presence does not mean every deployment enables all of them.
A response is not the same as a healthy application The health-check task file includes container, admin API, HTTP, HTTPS, metrics and certificate diagnostics. Several checks intentionally avoid failing the playbook. Some accept responses such as 404, 502 or 503 as well as successful status codes.
Those responses can establish that a proxy is reachable. They cannot establish that a user-facing application works. A useful deployment gate needs an expected response from the relevant application, not simply any response from the proxy.
There is another distinction worth keeping visible: the reviewed role entry point does not directly include the health-check task file. Its deployment summary leaves several health fields unset. A task file existing in a repository is not evidence that a particular deployment executed it.
Backup is a prerequisite, not a rollback guarantee The rollback tasks look for an available configuration backup, restore it when possible and attempt to restart the container. The role entry point places its rescue block after earlier task includes. I would not describe that as automatic recovery from every deployment failure.
For future changes, the checks I want are concrete: a known-good backup, a tested restoration path, explicit application-level health criteria, and a failure that actually stops promotion. This review does not claim those improvements have already been implemented.
Source basis: the private repository README, Terraform DNS resource declarations, and Caddy role entry-point, validation, health-check and rollback tasks. Operational configuration and secrets are omitted.
summary: A code-based look at my Caddy infrastructure: Terraform for VPS and DNS, Ansible for configuration, and the limits of deployment health checks.
title: My reverse proxy: separating provisioning, configuration and health checks

content:
antoinebou12/Artemis-Switch ★ 26 · 2 forks · Repository created 2026-08-08
GitHub statistics recorded 2026-10-20. A stream can report a healthy bitrate and still feel late. Artemis Switch is my Moonlight-Switch fork for Nintendo Switch, focused on the path between receiving a frame and presenting it. The useful question is not just “how fast is the decoder?” but “where did this frame wait?”
A client with a clear boundary Artemis builds on XITRIX/Moonlight-Switch: Borealis for the interface, the Moonlight/GameStream protocol for transport, FFmpeg/NVDEC for decoding, and deko3d for Switch presentation. Sunshine and Apollo remain PC hosts. Host administration stays in their own interfaces.
This distinction matters when debugging. A wrong virtual-display mode is a host issue; a growing decoded-frame queue belongs to the client. The repository documents host integrations, but that is not evidence that every host/device combination has passed hardware validation.
The frame pipeline flowchart TD H["PC host: Sunshine or Apollo"] --> N["Moonlight / GameStream transport"] N --> D["FFmpeg / NVDEC decode"] D --> Q["Decoded-frame queue"] Q --> S["Deadline and freshness selection"] S --> R["deko3d presentation"] R --> P["Switch display"] T["FramePipelineTelemetry"] -. measures .-> D T -. measures .-> Q T -. measures .-> R This is a simplified reading of the streaming code, not a claim about measured end-to-end input latency.
The subtle part: when to discard old frames LowLatencyFrameSelection.hpp checks the oldest frame’s deadline before advancing to the newest frame. Once the queue is eligible, it discards older frames and favors freshness. A backlog can bypass the ordinary gate so a stalled renderer catches up.
Why preserve that oldest deadline? If the gate follows the newest arriving frame, its deadline can keep moving forward. The queue receives frames, yet presentation starves. This small policy is more informative than a generic “low latency” label.
Measure stages separately FramePipelineTelemetry.hpp records decode timing, queue wait, client pipeline timing, render and GPU submission cost, actual video bitrate, and first-packet/decode/present milestones. It uses a monotonic clock and protects shared state with a mutex.
“Client pipeline” begins after network completion in this implementation. It does not include every host encoding, network transit, display scanout, and controller delay.
The README also describes Fit/Fill/Stretch presentation, FSR-style upscaling, RCAS sharpening, named stream profiles, and a performance overlay. These are controls to investigate tradeoffs, not a universal FPS promise.
What I would compare on hardware Keep the host, scene, resolution, and network fixed. Compare queue wait and present intervals with pacing options changed one at a time. Then test handheld and docked presentation separately. A lower average with worse spikes may still feel worse.
The project remains active. Its README explicitly separates portable tests and release builds from device validation. Read the installation and status notes before treating a compile result as a gameplay result.
Source trail Repository and screenshots Frame selection policy Pipeline telemetry Earlier handheld project overview
summary: Inside Artemis Switch: Moonlight transport, NVDEC, deko3d, frame pacing and the telemetry that makes streaming delays easier to diagnose.

antoinebou12/ComfyUI-UML ★ 3 · 3 forks · Repository created 2026-02-23
GitHub statistics recorded 2026-10-20. ComfyUI is useful beyond image generation when an intermediate result can become a node output. ComfyUI-UML applies that idea to diagrams: text enters a rendering node; an image, a saved file, and a shareable URL can leave it.
Keep the source in the workflow A screenshot is hard to revise. Mermaid or PlantUML source is much easier to inspect, compare, and regenerate. The node lets that source travel with the rest of a ComfyUI workflow instead of becoming an unexplained image.
The README documents 28 Kroki diagram types, with output formats validated per type. This does not mean every renderer supports every format.
flowchart TD T["Diagram text or optional LLM output"] --> N["Normalize diagram source"] N --> U["UMLDiagram node"] U --> K["Kroki web renderer"] U --> L["Optional local Mermaid / Graphviz"] K --> O["Image, file and URL outputs"] L --> O O --> P["PreviewImage or Diagram Viewer URL"] This is a conceptual view of the documented nodes, not a requirement to use an LLM.
What the code does with model output nodes/uml_diagram.py normalizes strings and several response shapes, extracts fenced diagram blocks, and prefers a block matching the selected type. That helps when a model returns prose around Mermaid code.
Extraction is not the same thing as syntax validation. A clean code block can still contain a broken diagram; the renderer must accept it.
From rendered bytes to a ComfyUI image Raster output is opened with Pillow, converted to RGB, normalized to floating-point values between zero and one, and wrapped as a tensor shaped [1, H, W, 3].
SVG is different. The code attempts a CairoSVG conversion for an image preview. For non-raster output without a successful conversion, it can return a tiny placeholder tensor while preserving the file output. That distinction explains why a saved SVG and its preview may behave differently.
Start with the smallest workflow comfy node install comfyui-uml Then restart ComfyUI and try the repository’s uml_single_diagram_only.json: UMLDiagram → PreviewImage. Add the viewer after rendering works. The repository also supplies Mermaid, PlantUML, and Ollama examples.
The web backend sends diagram source to the selected Kroki service. For sensitive architecture or offline use, the repository documents optional local Mermaid and Graphviz paths. Local Mermaid needs its JavaScript dependencies; SVG preview may need CairoSVG.
Source trail README, screenshot and installation Rendering node implementation Example workflows The MCP diagram project

AlgoETS/BatchBacktesting ★ 3 · 4 forks · Repository created 2023-03-29
GitHub statistics recorded 2026-10-20. A batch backtest is a small data pipeline: choose instruments, obtain prices, clean the observations, run a strategy, and save comparable results. AlgoETS/BatchBacktesting makes those steps visible in Python rather than hiding them behind a dashboard.
This image is an existing article illustration, not a new benchmark run.
Follow a single instrument first In src/BatchBacktesting.py, process_instrument selects a stock or crypto price adapter, cleans the data, and constructs a Backtest. It attaches the instrument and strategy names to the result before returning it.
flowchart TD I["Instrument list and strategy"] --> P["ThreadPoolExecutor"] P --> D["Fetch and clean historical data"] D --> B["Backtest per instrument"] B --> R["Result with Instrument and Strategy"] R --> C["Per-instrument CSV"] R --> A["Aggregate strategy CSV"] B --> H["Optional HTML chart"] The single-strategy runner defaults to four workers. Plot generation is optional. Those are code defaults, not measured throughput.
The assumptions are in the constructor The inspected runner uses 100,000 starting cash, 0.002 commission (0.2%), and exclusive orders. These settings belong beside any comparison of returns.
They still do not cover every market cost or data issue. Slippage, availability of short positions, delisted securities, and corporate actions need separate review.
An EMA detail worth noticing strategies.py computes 20-, 80-, and 150-period EMAs for the EMA class. Its entry decisions compare the 20 and 80 curves; the 150-period curve is calculated but not used in those next conditions.
The long-side rule closes the prior position and buys with a stop at 90% of the current price and a target at 125%. This is the implemented experiment, not a claim that those parameters are optimal.
Keep comparable rows together The runner writes per-instrument CSVs, an aggregate CSV per strategy, and optional HTML charts. The README links a published AAPL EMA chart covering 2018-04-04 through 2023-04-03. Those are that example’s dates, not a fixed range for every run.
Open the published AAPL example.
One analysis trap appears in analyse.py: groupby("Instrument").max() takes each column’s maximum independently. The resulting row can combine metrics from different runs. Select a real row by return before narrating its drawdown and duration.
Know the failure boundaries A failed instrument returns None. If all instruments fail, the later concatenation has no frames. The multi-strategy helper also creates an outer pool around inner pools, so API rate limits and nested concurrency deserve attention.
These are observations from reading the source. I did not rerun financial simulations for this article or generate new return claims.
Sources and related posts Repository and historical example Runner implementation Strategies Analysis helpers Earlier multi-ticker article
summary: Reading BatchBacktesting’s Python engine: worker pools, 0.2% commission, strategy defaults, CSV outputs and pitfalls in aggregate analysis.
title: Inside BatchBacktesting: parallel runs, explicit assumptions and useful outputs

antoinebou12/sm64coopdx-switch-N3DS ★ 3 · 1 forks · Repository created 2026-08-19
GitHub statistics recorded 2026-10-20. The interesting part of a console port is rarely a single compiler flag. sm64coopdx-switch-N3DS brings the Coop Deluxe engine to two very different handheld targets. The work lives at the platform boundary: graphics, input, audio, threading, and packaging.
This fork builds on the Coop Deluxe Team’s sm64coopdx, which continues djoslin0’s sm64ex-coop. The multiplayer engine and Lua ecosystem are upstream work; the console adapters are the focus here.
One engine, different platform services flowchart TD E["Shared CoopDX engine and Lua mods"] --> A["Platform APIs"] A --> S["Switch target"] A --> N["New 3DS target"] S --> SI["Switch controller backend"] S --> SN["Switch packaging and networking"] N --> G["Citro3D / PICA200 renderer"] N --> I["Circle Pad, C-Stick and touch"] N --> AU["NDSP audio and libctru threads"] The repository’s New 3DS port notes explicitly require that desktop and Switch builds gain no libctru, Citro3D, or devkitARM dependencies from the new target. That is the architectural constraint worth preserving.
New 3DS is a graphics translation problem The New 3DS backend implements CoopDX’s rendering API through Citro3D and PICA200. It translates common color-combiner paths into TEV stages, handles texture swizzling, depth, scissor, blending, and fog, and reports degraded combiner cases.
That last point matters. A backend that compiles is not automatically a faithful renderer. Explicit diagnostics tell you where the target GPU cannot represent an effect in the initial implementation.
The hardware foundation also separates the 400×240 top screen from the 320×240 bottom screen. Native controls map Circle Pad movement and C-Stick camera input. NDSP uses bounded buffers for stereo PCM16 audio.
Build the shell before the game There are two New 3DS paths: a small platform shell in Makefile.new3ds, and full-game integration in Makefile.new3ds-game.
make -f Makefile.new3ds port-smoke -j2 make -f Makefile.new3ds-game new3ds-integration-smoke -j2 These are documented compile checks, not commands I ran as part of writing this article. Separate Docker compose files and build subtrees keep the Switch and New 3DS toolchains apart.
Release files do not settle hardware status The README links a New 3DS release, while the detailed port notes still say not to call the port playable and describe hardware gameplay as unverified. Those signals should be read together: an artifact exists, but that alone does not establish stability or full multiplayer compatibility.
Switch documentation covers CoopNet, local wireless, an in-game keypad, crash diagnostics, and packaging. Consult the Switch installation guide for current instructions.
Builds require your own legally obtained North American SM64 ROM. This article supplies no ROM or extracted game assets.
Source trail Repository and README New 3DS architecture and verification status Switch build notes Switch controller adapter
summary: A code-based tour of the Switch and New 3DS CoopDX targets: graphics, controllers, audio, build isolation and current hardware-validation limits.

antoinebou12/Serilog.Sinks.SentrySDK ★ 2 · 0 forks · Repository created 2023-06-05
GitHub statistics recorded 2026-10-20. A log line tells you that something happened. An error event becomes useful when it also carries the exception, release, environment, and request context needed to investigate it. Serilog.Sinks.SentrySDK connects those two views.
This project is based on serilog-contrib/serilog-sinks-sentry. Its own GitHub stars measure interest in this repository, not total Serilog or Sentry adoption.
The adapter boundary flowchart TD A["Application"] --> L["Serilog LogEvent"] L --> S["SentrySink"] S --> W["ISentrySdkWrapper"] W --> SDK["Sentry .NET SDK"] SDK --> E["Sentry event reporting"] C["ASP.NET Core context middleware"] -. context .-> S SentrySink.cs implements ILogEventSink and IDisposable. An ISentrySdkWrapper abstracts message capture, exception capture, and transaction creation. That boundary also makes SDK interactions replaceable in tests.
Initialize once The sink configures Sentry internally. Its constructor rejects an empty DSN, prepares options, and owns an initialization handle. The README warns against adding a second independent SentrySdk.Init in the same process.
This is easy to miss in a web application that already initializes monitoring elsewhere. Decide who owns initialization before adding the sink.
dotnet add package Serilog.Sinks.SentrySDK The repository includes console and ASP.NET Core demos. Use their configuration examples for the installed version rather than copying an arbitrary overload from an older package.
Context needs deliberate handling The companion ASP.NET Core project contains a request adapter, destructuring policy, exception extensions, and context middleware. Request context helps diagnose failures, but it should be selected deliberately. Review PII settings and filtering before sending application data.
The sink exposes advanced options and a beforeSend callback. Its code documents callback ordering around EventId mapping; that is useful when filtering or enriching events without overwriting the sink’s own mapping.
Packages and adoption The current README describes two main package IDs that target net6.0 and net10.0, plus separate .6 and .10 variants. This describes package targets, not a recommendation about runtime support lifecycles.
The badge is a live download count for that package ID. It excludes the separately published variants, and downloads are not the same as active installations. The dated repository snapshot above is kept separate.
What the checks establish The README documents xUnit tests, coverage collection, and formatting checks. CI and release badges are linked evidence; this article does not claim those checks were rerun here or invent a coverage percentage.
Sources README and package matrix Sink implementation Console and web demos NuGet package statistics
summary: A tour of the Serilog Sentry sink: SDK initialization, event handling, ASP.NET Core context, NuGet packages and observable project activity.

AlgoETS/Workshop1 ★ 3 · 0 forks · Repository created 2023-09-07
GitHub statistics recorded 2026-10-20. The most useful beginner workshop gives each new concept somewhere to go. AlgoETS/Workshop1 moves from Python setup to an API response, a DataFrame, and a chart. The final notebook uses Apple price data and exponential moving averages to bring those steps together.
Nine notebooks, six stages The repository contains nine Jupyter notebooks across six numbered directories: two setup notebooks, two Python notebooks, one API notebook, one pandas notebook, two visualization notebooks, and one final project.
This is a count of checked-in teaching material, not a student attendance or completion statistic.
flowchart TD S["Environment and cloud notebooks"] --> P["Python basics and advanced concepts"] P --> A["Read API responses"] A --> D["Clean and explore with pandas"] D --> V["Visualize the data"] V --> E["Apple prices and EMA project"] Keep setup from swallowing the lesson The README links a Colab entry point. Local Jupyter is also documented. Offering both lets learners begin with code while keeping environment setup available as its own topic.
The six-stage structure makes it possible to return to a missing concept without restarting the entire project.
The final exercise is concrete The code in 5.1_project_ema.ipynb plots Apple closing prices with 12-, 26-, 50-, 100-, and 200-day EMA curves. This is a more precise description than the README’s broad “advanced exploration and modeling” language.
The exercise connects a request, tabular data, indicator columns, and a labeled chart. It does not establish that any crossover makes money.
Read the chart as a data exercise Useful classroom questions are technical: are dates ordered correctly? Were missing values removed intentionally? Why does a longer EMA respond more slowly? Are all curves computed from the same observations?
API availability, keys, and package versions can change since the original workshop. The notebooks are teaching material to inspect and adapt, not a promise of a fresh one-command environment.
From one chart to a batch experiment The natural continuation is BatchBacktesting: the same indicator idea, now evaluated across instruments with recorded assumptions and comparable outputs.
That progression keeps the focus on understanding data and code before interpreting a leaderboard.
Sources Workshop repository and original artwork Python basics notebook EMA project code

uml-mcp gives an MCP client real diagram tools: an assistant supplies Mermaid, PlantUML, or another supported diagram source, and the server returns rendered output and useful links. The current repository documents five tools and a catalog of roughly 37 Kroki-backed types. Those counts describe the documented interface, not a rendering benchmark. Version française.
antoinebou12/uml-mcp ★ 107 · 29 forks · Repository created 2025-04-01
GitHub statistics recorded 2026-10-20. From Mermaid source to image and editor links sequenceDiagram participant C as MCP client participant U as UML-MCP participant R as Renderer C->>U: generate_uml with source and type U->>U: Check request U->>R: Build rendering request R-->>U: Rendered diagram U-->>C: URL, editor link or image tools/kroki/mermaid.py builds JSON state, compresses it with zlib, and encodes it as URL-safe base64. That state supports both an image link and an editable mermaid.live link.
The module distinguishes SVG at /svg/ from PNG/JPEG/WebP at /img/?type=.... A wrong endpoint can break a perfectly valid diagram before its syntax ever becomes the problem.
The repository also exposes generate_uml_image, validate_uml, list_diagram_types, and generate_uml_batch. Choose the tool for inline preview, source checks, format discovery, or multiple independent renders.
There is an operations side too The current README documents uml-mcp admin, metrics, and a Kroki playground. They help separate invalid source, unavailable renderers, and configuration problems. A successful request still needs a human check that the diagram represents the intended system.
For the same diagram-source idea inside a node editor, see ComfyUI-UML.
Why MCP instead of copy-paste templates? I started with ChatGPT plugins (D2C OpenAI diagram plugin) and AIPRM sequence templates. Both work, but editors wanted native tools: enable a server once, call generate_uml from the agent, save .mmd + SVG beside the post. MCP is that layer — same idea as the plugin, different host.
What it supports Backend Good for Mermaid GitHub-native flows, quick sequences PlantUML Classic UML, deployments, strict notation Kroki Unified render path when you mix formats Hosted endpoint: uml-mcp.vercel.app/mcp. Docs site: antoinebou12.github.io/uml-mcp.
Cursor setup (short) Clone or install from github.com/antoinebou12/uml-mcp (README has the MCP config block). Add the server to Cursor MCP settings. Ask for a diagram type explicitly — e.g. “Mermaid sequence: user, React, FastAPI, Postgres, login with cache miss.” I use it across this blog for pipeline and career diagrams; see AI figurines post or software engineering journey for examples.
Limits Models still hallucinate syntax sometimes — always render locally before publishing. Secrets belong out of prompts; diagram user/service names, not production credentials. OpenAI plugin churn moved the ChatGPT story toward Custom GPT + MCP; treat the D2C plugin post as historical context with a live successor. Project page More badges and links: uml-mcp project page.

Three repos I maintain on the side: Artemis-Switch for Apollo/Sunshine streaming on Switch, moonlight-N3DS for GameStream on New 3DS, and sm64coopdx-switch as a Switch build of cooperative Super Mario 64. They share the same itch — run something interesting on hardware that was not designed for it — but the stack and constraints differ. Version française.
Artemis-Switch — PC streaming on Switch Artemis-Switch is my fork of XITRIX/Moonlight-Switch, wired for Apollo (Sunshine) hosts instead of classic NVIDIA GameStream. I stream Steam Big Picture from my desktop (AntoinePC) and use the in-app overlay for quick host shortcuts and a live performance panel.
The Quick tab exposes window-management shortcuts (Win+Shift+Left / Right), keyboard presets, and Apollo host scripts without leaving the stream. Handy when the host is a Windows box and the Switch is just the display.
Performance shows bitrate (~12 Mbps in this capture), Switch Wi-Fi bars, and receive / decode / render timings. Render is usually the bottleneck on Switch; sub-millisecond receive and decode means the network and decoder are healthy and the frame budget is mostly compositing.
Repo: github.com/antoinebou12/Artemis-Switch (★ 12). Upstream Moonlight-Switch work also shows up on my CV as merged toolchain fixes for newer devkitPro toolchains — separate from the Artemis fork, same Moonlight lineage.
moonlight-N3DS — GameStream on New 3DS moonlight-N3DS tracks zoeyjodon/moonlight-N3DS, a GameStream client for New 3DS (extra RAM and CPU vs OG 3DS). My fork is where I experiment with build fixes and integration; star count on my repo is still low — the community interest lives on upstream (~300★), which is the right place to look for installs and issues.
Constraints are brutal: 400×240 top screen, software decode, Wi-Fi on a 2015 handheld. Expect lower bitrate and higher latency than Switch; the win is having any Moonlight path on 3DS at all.
Repo: github.com/antoinebou12/moonlight-N3DS.
sm64coopdx-switch — co-op Mario 64 on Switch sm64coopdx-switch ports coop-deluxe/sm64coopdx to Switch homebrew. sm64coopdx is the continuation of sm64ex-coop: online co-op, Lua mods, and QoL the decomp scene added over years.
Legal note: like every SM64 port, you must supply your own legally obtained ROM. The repo builds the port; it does not ship game assets.
Repo: github.com/antoinebou12/sm64coopdx-switch.

content:
Couplage contact-apparence pour l’usure de surfaces microstructurées en simulation interactive — my ÉTS master’s thesis (English abstract title: Visual Appearance Evolution from Wear on Microstructured Surfaces in Texture Space). Directed by Sheldon Andrews, defended 14 August 2026. The core idea: give material maps a persistent local memory of contact. Body travel alone cannot predict where wear shows up. Version française.
The gap Real surfaces keep a trace of friction and slip. Interactive simulators usually throw that away at the end of each timestep. The contact solver already computes impulses, relative velocity, tangential traction, and dissipation — then updates rigid-body motion and stops. Material maps (albedo, roughness, normals) stay fixed unless an artist paints wear by hand.
The thesis closes that loop: mechanical contact resolution feeds texture-space appearance evolution at the places contact actually happened.
Pipeline (one glance) Sparse contacts are grouped into local patches, projected into material atlases, and reconstructed as tangential velocity, effective traction, and frictional dissipation on a GPU patch grid. Those fields drive accumulation of sliding distance, dominant direction, and wear — then progressive map updates without global remeshing.
Source: wear-pipeline-flow.mmd (same chain as GraphQuon 2025). The interactive implementation in TextureFriction adds a stricter runtime order: pre-solve FBO passes → PGS or AVBD solve → post-solve velocity/traction → sliding/wear/direction deposit → rendering.
Three contributions Dissipation-based local accumulation — links sliding, reconstructed traction, and visual surface evolution in texture space. Contact-to-atlas projection architecture — patch clustering, GPU buffers, persistent material memory on a fixed mesh; sliding, direction, and wear written where overlap says contact occurred. GelSight acquisition and comparison — controlled wear bench captures build the Wear Surface Texture Datasets and calibrate simulated patterns against measured microgeometry. Two codebases Repo Role WearPaper LaTeX thesis sources, ACM article, Beamer defense slides, and canonical bibliography. TextureFriction (local, E:\master\TextureFriction) Qt6 + OpenGL 4.3+ simulator: PGS/AVBD contact, cluster FBO passes, GPU deposition into sliding/wear/direction atlases. Build: just build, run: just run-build. See docs/architecture/14-thesis-pipeline-and-rationale.md in the repo. WearPaper is the paper trail; TextureFriction is where the loop runs at interactive rates.
Validation Acquisitions on a reciprocal abrasion bench feed measured normal maps and staged wear progression. Public dataset: ETSim/WearSurfacesDatasets. Surface metrology tooling connects to my CV work on TrueMapData and surfalize integration.
Results (snapshot) In tested scenarios, written texels track cumulative wear more closely than body travel alone; contact topology changes the deposit pattern. A cube or torus on a plane stays within an interactive budget; cost rises sharply when several contact groups are processed together. The method is a physically motivated appearance model, not a full tribology simulator — limits remain around effective-field reconstruction, calibration, and UV parameterization.
Research materials The manuscript sources, article, and defense slides live in ETSim/WearPaper.
Related GraphQuon 2025 — Where to Wear? — conference talk on the same research line Software engineering journey — ÉTS master’s thread (rendering, physics, wear) CV education line: Thesis: real-time surface wear in interactive physics simulations, with dynamic friction and textures
summary: ÉTS master's thesis on real-time surface wear in interactive simulation — frictional dissipation, GPU texture atlases, GelSight validation, WearPaper and TextureFriction.

content:
Good 2D toy art beats a fancy image-to-3D model. This post walks the steps in order, links a slide deck, a ComfyUI workflow, and how I sketch the flow with uml-mcp.
Pipeline (in order) Reference photo — clear side or front view. Chibi vinyl render — ChatGPT, Midjourney, or ComfyUI (OmniGen2). Mesh — Hunyuan3D v2 (local ComfyUI or hosted tools). Print — orient, supports, resin slice; fix islands with UVtools if needed. Pipeline sequence (source: figurine-pipeline-sequence.mmd, rendered with uml-mcp):
sequenceDiagram autonumber actor User participant Photo as Reference photo participant ComfyUI participant OmniGen2 as OmniGen2 stage participant Hunyuan3D as Hunyuan3D v2 stage participant Slicer as Resin slicer participant Printer User->>Photo: Side or front reference User->>ComfyUI: Load chibi workflow + reference-photo.jpg ComfyUI->>OmniGen2: ReferenceLatent + chibi vinyl prompt OmniGen2-->>ComfyUI: PNG (white background) ComfyUI->>Hunyuan3D: CLIPVision + image-to-mesh Hunyuan3D-->>ComfyUI: GLB (VoxelToMesh 0.7 / 0.6) ComfyUI-->>User: mesh/ComfyUI*.glb User->>Slicer: Orient, supports, hollow Slicer-->>User: Sliced job User->>Printer: Resin print Printer-->>User: Chibi figurine Deck (~17 MB) — screenshots and tool URLs from the talk:
Download slide deck (.pptx)(~17 MB) In-browser preview via Microsoft Office Online. If it fails to load, use the download link above (large decks may not preview).
Step 1 — 2D toy / chibi Deck prompt:
Convert this image into a toy-style plastic figure. Keep features but simplify and smoothen as if molded in plastic.
Chibi prompt (same idea, bigger head):
Vinyl chibi figurine, smooth plastic, white background, one character, pose that can stand on a base.
Gallery (ChatGPT):
Document the flow — uml-mcp The sequence diagram above was generated with uml-mcp (generate_uml, type mermaid) and saved as figurine-pipeline-sequence.mmd + SVG in this page bundle.
In Cursor: enable the uml-mcp server (repo README), then call generate_uml with the .mmd source or ask for a sequence diagram of the ComfyUI → print steps. Same idea as ChatGPT sequence diagrams.
Step 2 — ComfyUI (one graph) Download: image_omnigen2_image_edit.json — Load in ComfyUI (OmniGen2 chibi edit + Hunyuan3D v2 mesh). Put your photo in input/ as reference-photo.jpg (or edit the LoadImage node).
Stage What it does A OmniGen2 + ReferenceLatent → chibi PNG (heun, 45 steps) B Hunyuan3D v2 → two GLBs (mesh/ComfyUI*.glb, thresholds 0.7 and 0.6) Full positive/negative prompts and seeds are in the JSON. Needs OmniGen2 + Hunyuan3D-2 custom nodes (Hunyuan3D-2). On 8–12 GB VRAM, lower octree_resolution or num_chunks.
Step 3 — Image to 3D (hosted) Single-image mesh tools — clarity of the toy PNG matters more than the brand.
Tool Link Notes Hunyuan3D-2 GitHub Open weights / local or hosted runs; strong general image-to-3D. RodinHD WebGL demo High-detail avatars and figurines from images. Hi3DGen Hugging Face demo 2D diffusion prior + geometry consistency (CHI 2024 paper, white paper PDF). Hyper3D hyper3d.ai Fast commercial image-to-3D. Meshy meshy.ai Text/image to 3D with editing and remeshing. Tripo3D studio.tripo3d.ai Browser studio workflow. Sparc3D lizhihao6.github.io/Sparc3D Structured sparse-view reconstruction. Hi3DGen (CHI 2024, demo) — strong when the 2D silhouette is already clean.
Mesh preview Sample GLB files from Hunyuan3D, RodinHD, Hyper3D, and Hi3DGen are not stored in this repo (each was 20–75 MB). Use the generator previews in the tool UIs, or export from your own ComfyUI run (mesh/ComfyUI*.glb).
Step 4 — Mesh settings Tune face count, symmetry, and remesh in the generator UI before export.
Step 5 — Resin print Resin for small parts. Tilt overhangs toward the plate; light supports on hair and capes.
Check floating islands with the slicer or UVtools before printing.
Printed results When to use this pipeline Goal Start here Gift figurine from a pet photo ChatGPT/Midjourney chibi → hosted mesh Repeatable local batch ComfyUI JSON in this bundle Teaching a class Deck + uml-mcp sequence diagram Production CAD interchange Expect cleanup in Blender after GLB Pitfalls Skipping 2D quality — mesh tools amplify bad silhouettes. Committing 50 MB GLBs — export locally; link tools instead. Zero island check — resin failures mid-print waste hours. content:
I taught a thread on “find movies like this” that kept growing: embeddings in PostgreSQL, the same idea in Qdrant with two different vector meanings, then retrieval + a local LLM grounded on the same rows. This page is the story; notebooks and animations live in AlgoETS/SimilityVectorEmbedding. Version française.
AlgoETS/SimilityVectorEmbedding ★ 1 · 0 forks · Repository created 2024-05-06
GitHub statistics recorded 2026-10-20. The original demos These three animations come from the project README. They show recorded interfaces and processing steps, not current latency measurements.
Gradio interface: exploring similar movies.
Still from the Gradio UI — single-title search.
Generating vector representations with Sentence Transformers.
t-SNE of movie embeddings — cluster structure in 2D.
The Qdrant search and recommendation workflow.
Graph view: Superman neighborhood, genres, and cast centrality.
What the notebooks actually build postgres/1.create_table.ipynb combines title, year, genres, actors, director, summary, and country into model input. It compares five model configurations: BART, GTE, MiniLM-L12, RoBERTa, and e5-large. This is a code inventory, not an accuracy ranking.
qdrant/0.simple.ipynb creates a 384-dimensional collection with cosine distance and upserts batches of 100 points. The dimension must match the selected encoder. The notebook recreates its collection, so inspect that step before using an existing database.
flowchart TD J["movies.json metadata"] --> T["Combined and preprocessed text"] T --> E["Selected encoder"] E --> N["Normalize vectors"] N --> P["PostgreSQL / pgvector"] N --> Q["Qdrant vector collection"] R["Query encoded with the same model"] --> P R --> Q P --> K["Nearest movies"] Q --> K K --> G["Interface and explanation"] This editable Mermaid replaces a static architecture screenshot. It summarizes the shared dense-vector path without pretending different encoders share one interchangeable vector space.
The question behind all three parts Recommendation systems usually hide three different questions:
Plot language — “films that feel like this description.” Taste overlap — “users who rated like you.” Explainability — “why these titles?” with text the user asked. Parts 1–3 map to those questions. Mixing them without labeling the vector type is how demos lie.
Part 1 — PostgreSQL, pgvector, and honest SQL Build the catalog Start from structured movie JSON (movies.json in the course repo). Concatenate title, year, genres, cast, summary; encode with Sentence Transformers (MiniLM, GTE, etc.); store typed vector columns beside relational fields.
Why pgvector? Vectors stay next to SQL you already trust. Distance operators (<=> cosine, <-> L2) turn kNN into ORDER BY … LIMIT.
SELECT title, 1 - (embedding_minilm <=> ( SELECT embedding_minilm FROM movies WHERE title = $1 )) AS similarity FROM movies WHERE title IS DISTINCT FROM $1 ORDER BY similarity DESC LIMIT 10; Swap column names per model — the course keeps several embedding_* columns to compare neighborhoods side by side.
What students learn here Normalizing embeddings for cosine. How choice of encoder shifts “similar” (BART vs MiniLM vs e5-large). That SQL transparency beats a black-box API when you are debugging wrong neighbors. Full plots and distribution charts: Medium Part 1 and postgres/ notebooks in the repo.
Part 2 — Qdrant, MovieLens, dense vs sparse Same “similarity in vector space,” different semantics:
Collection Vector type Question it answers Movies Dense text embedding “Like this wording / vibe” Users (profile) Dense User representation in same space (seed pipeline) Ratings Sparse movieId → rating “Users with overlapping taste” Dense path: encode query text with MiniLM, search movies collection — mirrors Part 1 but in Qdrant’s API.
Sparse path: build NamedSparseVector from a user’s ratings, find similar users, aggregate their high scores on unseen movies — collaborative filtering without training a neural net in the notebook.
FastAPI teaching project (movie_recommendation in the course repo) exposes both flows to a simple HTML UI.
Starter notebook: qdrant/0.simple.ipynb before MovieLens scale.
Part 3 — RAG with LangChain + Ollama Reuse pgvector rows as evidence:
flowchart LR Q[User question] --> E[Embed question] E --> SQL[kNN in SQL] SQL --> Rows[Top movies] Rows --> LLM[Ollama via LangChain] LLM --> A[Grounded answer] Pipeline: HuggingFaceEmbeddings → SQL ordering by <=> on embedding_MiniLM → prompt that includes schema + retrieved rows → Ollama(model="llama2:13b-chat").
The saved notebook output is instructive because it fails politely:
LangChain warns on unknown vector column types. The LLM sometimes emits SQL that is not valid pgvector. Heavy models timeout under load. RAG is not “embed and forget” — you need validation, smaller models, or hybrid retrieval.
Notebook: postgres/3.LLMS.ipynb.
When not to use this stack Situation Better path Cold-start users with no ratings Dense metadata only Billion-scale sparse CF Specialized CF stack, not demo Qdrant Sub-10 ms latency at huge QPS Managed vector DB + tuning Legal need for exact quotes RAG + citation checks, not raw LLM Takeaway Embed → store → nearest neighbors three times, with three meanings of “neighbor.” Part 3 teaches humility: generators drift from executable SQL unless you constrain them.

content:
I took part in QcES (Spring 2024 cohort) while working through lean discovery: business model canvas, customer interviews, short pitches, and everything in between. This post is my own recap—not an official program document. Full article in French if you prefer.
What stuck with me The program kept coming back to a few ideas. The Business Model Canvas is a shared map for how you create, deliver, and capture value—and whether the idea is desirable, feasible, and viable. You usually start with who you serve and what you promise them, then revise as the market talks back.
Segmentation sounds dry until you try pitching to “doctors” or “parents.” Splitting B2B (firmographics) from B2C (demographics, behavior) makes the market something you can actually reach.
Interviews are for learning, not closing a sale. The facilitators repeated it until it landed: connect, don’t convince; stay curious about the problem, not married to your first solution.
Short feedback rounds (one real strength, one growth angle) and a ~90 second pitch without slides force clarity early. A roadmap is a strategic view over time—not a Gantt chart. And PoC, prototype, and MVP are different beats: can it work, how do people interact, what is the smallest thing you can put in front of real users.
For pitching, Hook → Believe → Join showed up again and again: problem first, then why you’re credible, then a specific ask.
How the pieces connect You do not fill the canvas once and frame it. You state a hypothesis, talk to people, adjust segments and value proposition, decide what belongs on a roadmap, then practice explaining it out loud.
flowchart LR hyp[Hypothesis] --> int[Interview] int --> ins[Insight] ins --> bmc[BMC and segment] bmc --> road[Roadmap] road --> pit[Pitch] Business model canvas Nine blocks, one page: segments, value proposition, channels, relationships, revenue, resources, activities, partners, costs. The point is not decoration—it is survival. Every block can break you if you ignore it, and the canvas should move when customers or competitors shift.
We were pushed to nail for whom and how you help before optimizing the rest. That matches the hypothesis–validation loop: test beliefs about the customer and the problem, not only the tech stack.
Customer segments Who pays is not always who uses. An early customer often has a real problem, knows it, is looking for options, maybe already hacked a workaround, and might have budget.
B2B segments lean on company size, sector, and buying dynamics. B2C adds lifestyle and behavior. The win is replacing vague labels with groups you can find, email, and interview.
Sharing the idea Ninety seconds, no deck: state the problem in plain language, who benefits, what you offer, and why it matters. You are not expected to quote TAM on day one—it is a clarity filter.
When you receive feedback, listen to understand. When you give it, name something that works, then one concrete “what would make this stronger.”
Interviews This was the heart of the cohort for me. Interviews fill the gaps a first canvas always has. Do not pitch your fix on the call—learn how the other person lives the problem.
Talk to people beyond the “ideal customer”: users of substitutes, experts, suppliers, communities. Discovery does not end after three calls; it continues through pivots.
Finding people, booking time, and running a useful conversation are skills. The line I still repeat: fall in love with the problem, not the solution.
Roadmap, PoC, prototype, MVP A roadmap answers where you are headed for a given audience (team, investors, partners) over a chosen horizon. It is not the same as a detailed project plan.
Proof of concept checks whether the approach can work. A prototype explores interaction—often before a real launch. An MVP is the smallest version you put in front of real users to learn fast, including from what breaks.
Roadmaps look different in discovery, validation, and growth. That alone saved me from over-planning too early.
Market and value proposition Market work is more than counting accounts. Macro forces, industry dynamics, customer behavior, and trends set constraints and openings.
Value proposition is offer plus customer benefit—what you deliver and why someone cares. Pain points and “why now” become interview questions, not slide filler.
Pitching: Hook, Believe, Join A pitch asks for a next step: time, intros, lab access, funding. Formats vary; structure helps.
Hook — the problem and why it matters to a real audience. Do not open with the product. Believe — the solution, differentiation, evidence (traction, team, recent wins). Join — a specific ask: money, expertise, partnership, introduction. A simple ~90 second scaffold: who you are, problem, offer for a target, value proposition, contrast with alternatives, recent milestone, call to action.
What I would tell a founder friend Stage Do this Skip this Week 1 Write who hurts and how you will find them Logo and LLC debate Week 2–3 Five interviews, same script Pitching strangers your solution Week 4 Update BMC once with evidence Fake revenue line in slides Before demo day 90 s pitch aloud daily Adding a fifteenth feature Related posts Professional résumé + JSON Resume — packaging the same story for hiring MarketWatch Python library — side project born from AlgoÉTS energy Closing QcES tied tools to habits: canvas, segmentation, roadmap on one side; interviews, feedback, pitching on the other. The thread is keeping the problem central, making assumptions testable, and speaking clearly enough that people can help—not just nod.
If you are in a similar program, a few well-run interviews usually teach more than a perfectly styled canvas. Consistency beats polish.

I wanted to automate chores in MarketWatch’s virtual stock game (paper trading, not a real broker). marketwatch on PyPI is the small client I shipped — watchlists, game state, portfolio, orders, leaderboard. Version française.
Why build this Course and side projects already used BatchBacktesting on historical data — see experimentation with indicators. MarketWatch’s game is a different beast: session cookies, game rules, and leaderboards that change with the semester. A thin Python wrapper beat curl scripts in a notebook.
I also wanted a documented surface for teammates: “here is how you list games” beats sharing a gist that rots when the HTML form changes. The package is intentionally small — no ORM, no strategy engine — just HTTP shaped like the site.
Design choices Choice Reason Class-based client One login, many calls in a script Explicit methods per endpoint Easier to grep when MarketWatch changes a path Docs on GitHub Pages PyPI description alone is too short for auth edge cases No bundled strategies Keeps the library neutral; strategies belong in your repo Links Package: pypi.org/project/marketwatch Documentation: antoinebou12.github.io/marketwatch Source & issues: github.com/antoinebou12/marketwatch What it can do Area Methods (see docs for signatures) Watchlists Create, list, update symbols Games List games, read settings Portfolio Positions, pending orders Trading Buy / sell inside game rules Social Leaderboard for a game Useful for small bots and screening inside the game — not HFT, not brokerage.
Quick start pip install marketwatch from marketwatch import MarketWatch mw = MarketWatch("your_username", "your_password") mw.get_games() mw.get_price("AAPL") Login edge cases (2FA absent, session expiry) are documented on the site — read before cron-scheduling anything.
Limits and responsibility Unofficial API — HTML/JSON endpoints can change; pin versions and expect breakage. Terms of use — automation may conflict with MarketWatch rules; use for learning, not abuse. Not financial advice — paper gains do not validate a strategy; pair with honest backtests on separate data. For research-style batch runs on many tickers, see multiple indicators backtesting and Monte Carlo risk bands.

Version française.
What I presented Talk title: Where to Wear? (subtitle on the opening slide: Every surface has a biography written by frictional contact).
The story is simple to state and hard to simulate: time, contact, and energy dissipation change how a surface looks and behaves—from bathroom tile wear patterns at an engineering school to scratches on tools, gaming materials, and robotics grippers. The deck walks from motivation through mechanics (Archard wear, energy-based wear laws), a graphics-oriented pipeline (contact mask, orthographic volumes, tangential velocity and traction, texture integration), and validation ideas (GelSight capture, materials atlas interpolation).
Pipeline (one glance) Rendered with uml-mcp from wear-pipeline-flow.mmd:
Why it fit GraphQuon GraphQuon is where Quebec and Ontario graphics labs share work before SIGGRAPH season—short talks, posters, and honest feedback from people who build simulators and renderers. After helping with the GraphQuon 2024 site at ÉTS, presenting in Toronto in 2025 felt like the same community on the other side of the drive.
The research line connects to my ÉTS work on 3D fabrication and validation of frictional surfaces (project description).

content:
Blender add-ons that need NumPy, meshio, or requests hit the same wall: Blender ships its own Python, so system pip does nothing useful. I wrote a small installer that targets Blender’s sys.executable, drops wheels under scripts/modules, and runs in a background thread so the UI stays responsive (Blender 4.2+, Windows). Version française.
The problem in one sentence You cannot pip install globally and expect import meshio inside Blender — the interpreter path is Blender’s bundled runtime.
Strategy Piece Role sys.executable Invoke pip against Blender’s Python bpy.utils.user_resource("SCRIPTS", path="modules") Writable install dir per user/version site.addsitedir Make imports resolve next launch Background thread + bpy.app.timers Avoid freezing the UI; show popups when done The installer script (core idea) REQUIRED_PACKAGES = { "fileseq": "fileseq==1.15.2", "meshio": "meshio==5.3.4", "rich": "rich==13.7.0", "requests": "requests==2.31.0", } def install_package(package, modules_path): subprocess.check_call([ sys.executable, "-m", "pip", "install", "--upgrade", "--target", modules_path, package, ]) Full script in the Medium article and my repo copies — includes progress bar hooks and __import__ checks to skip already-installed wheels.
How to run it Option A — Scripting workspace: paste in Text Editor → Run Script → wait for popup.
Option B — Add-on register():
def register(): modules_path = get_modules_path() append_modules_to_sys_path(modules_path) background_install_packages(REQUIRED_PACKAGES, modules_path) Ship dependencies with your add-on so users are not guessing which Python to use.
Troubleshooting Restart Blender after first install. print(sys.path) if imports fail — confirm modules is listed. Version pin wheels — Blender’s Python version is not your system 3.12. When not to use this pattern Case Why Add-on targets many Blender versions Pin and test per minor version Heavy CUDA stacks May exceed user GPU/driver setup Corporate locked-down PCs pip may be blocked — vendor wheels manually Takeaway Automate dependency install inside Blender’s sandbox; users stop emailing “which Python?” — you own the matrix in REQUIRED_PACKAGES.
Related posts Skate rack — CAD to plywood — physical maker pipeline AI figurines / 3D print — mesh tools in another ecosystem References Blender API Managing Python in Blender Python packaging guide Originally published on Medium.
summary: Install pip packages into Blender’s embedded Python — user modules folder, background thread, popups — without breaking the core install.
title: A Method to Install Python Packages for Add-ons & Plugins in Blender (Windows, Blender 4.2+)

GraphQuon (formerly MOTOGRAPH) is the annual Quebec–Ontario pre-SIGGRAPH workshop for East-Canadian computer graphics labs. The 2024 edition ran 9–10 November 2024 at École de technologie supérieure (ÉTS) in Montréal. I helped build and host the conference website at graphquon.github.io so schedules, registration, and past editions stayed in one place. Version française.
What GraphQuon is for From the site’s About the event copy: students present prospective SIGGRAPH-bound work to a friendly, constructively critical audience and get feedback before the real submission crunch. Faculty groups across Quebec and Ontario rotate hosting; 2024 was ÉTS’s turn.
Questions for organizers: graphquon@etsmtl.ca.

A few anchors I remember from the published program:
Saturday 9 November
Morning talks included Quoc-Minh Ton-That, Melissa Katz (McGill), and Ivan Puhachov (UdeM) among the honourable mentions. Midday ÉTS/Sherbrooke block: Justin Benoist, Arthur Delon, Joel Pelletier-Guenette. Afternoon: Abhishek Madan (Toronto); Clara Kim (Waterloo) won Best presentation. Sunday 10 November
Morning honourable mentions included Victor Rong, Ryusuke Sugimoto, Yue Chang, and Ege Ciklabakkal. Late afternoon ÉTS/MILA block: Alex Hoang-Cao, Darsh Kaushik. The room itself matched the workshop vibe: ÉTS auditorium, red carpet, simple stage, and a lot of white chairs filled between sessions.
Hallway highlight: Masha Shugrina (NVIDIA) Between sessions I talked with Masha Shugrina (NVIDIA Spatial Intelligence Lab / creative AI tools). Two demos stuck with me:
Diffusion Texture Painting (SIGGRAPH 2024) — painting on UV-mapped meshes with a diffusion brush so strokes stay seamless and you can blend complex reference textures interactively, not just stamp pixels. A Gaussian-splat style environment scan — a simple scene you could walk around in, the kind of collider/scan setup that makes spatial content feel immediate without a heavy offline pipeline. (NVIDIA’s newer line of work includes Gaussian splat painting research; the booth conversation was about that direction more than a single paper title.) It was the useful kind of industry chat: concrete tools you could imagine plugging into a lab pipeline, not a slide deck of buzzwords.
Audience and vibe Mostly graphics + vision grad students and faculty from Quebec and Ontario — people who understand meshes and shaders but still want a friendly room. Talks skewed research-heavy; questions were about evaluation protocols and whether a method would survive a SIGGRAPH reviewer, not startup pitch decks.
My role vs 2025 For 2024 I was on the organizing/web side (site on GitHub Pages, schedule pages, contact blocks). That meant I learned the boring critical path: bios on time, PDF links that do not 404, and a schedule page that works on mobile in a hallway. In 2025 I presented at the Toronto edition — see GraphQuon 2025 — University of Toronto (Where to Wear? with Sheldon Andrews). Organizing first made presenting calmer — I already knew where the HDMI adapter lived.
Tips if you attend next year Bring a question for the presenters — honourable mentions get sharp feedback when they name what they want (SIGGRAPH track, clarity, eval). Talk in the hall — half the value is comparing pipelines with other Quebec/Ontario labs. Check the site early — schedules shift; graphquon.github.io is the source of truth. content:
Same BatchBacktesting engine as the earlier indicator experiment, but emphasized at portfolio scale: many tickers, two strategies, equities plus crypto, aggregate winners and losers. Version française.
Why run many tickers at once Single-ticker backtests flatter you. A grid run answers:
Does this rule only work on one heroic symbol? Are disasters clustered in a sector or era? Is crypto dominating the leaderboard because volatility is unbounded in the sim? Architecture (same as BatchBacktesting) Layer Role Data adapters FMP + Binance fetch Strategy objects EMA, MACD parameter sets Runner Thread pool, CSV output, optional plots output/ Per-run artifacts — not committed to GitHub by default Pre-calculated results are not in the upstream repo (too user-specific). You generate locally, then inspect output/charts/....
Running at scale run_backtests(get_SP500(), strategy=EMA, num_threads=12, generate_plots=True) run_backtests(get_SP500(), strategy=MACD, num_threads=12, generate_plots=True) run_backtests(get_all_crypto(), strategy=EMA, num_threads=12, generate_plots=True) run_backtests(get_all_crypto(), strategy=MACD, num_threads=12, generate_plots=True) Tune num_threads to your machine and API rate limits.
Reading leaderboard extremes (EMA example) High returns often mix:
Long bullish windows on leveraged crypto pairs. Mean-reversion false signals in sideways stocks (sometimes lucky). Parameters tuned implicitly by the default strategy class. Deep negatives flag:
Illiquid symbols where the sim still trades. Trend rules in collapsing sectors. Stablecoins or broken pairs treated like normal tickers. Before narrating “MACD beats EMA,” compare median return, not only top decile.
Honest limitations Not financial advice. Fees, borrow, halts, and corporate actions are only as good as the data feed + library defaults. Past batch output ≠ future edge. Takeaway Use multi-ticker backtests as smoke tests for rules — find where they break, not where to deploy capital.

content:
I collect LEGO and write Python — so I merged Rebrickable exports with a BrickEconomy scraper to see how sets, colors, and themes evolved, and whether a simple model could explain prices on classics like 001-1. This page is the story with charts; full notebooks live in AlgoETS/LegosTracker. Version française.
Data sources Dataset What it gives you Rebrickable CSVs sets, themes, parts, colors, inventories — great for counts and joins BrickEconomy (scraped) historical resale-style prices Rebrickable does not ship Rebrickable files include sets.csv, themes.csv, parts.csv, colors.csv, and inventory tables — standard star schema for “how big is LEGO over time?”
Sets over the decades Two trends jump out when you group by year:
Count of named sets rises — LEGO product line expansion is real in the data. Average part count per set climbs — models got denser, not just more numerous. Narrative check: adult-targeted lines and licensed themes show up as tail mass in part counts, not only kid-scale sets.
Themes — what dominates the catalog Join sets.theme_id → themes, filter to top-level themes (no parent_id), bar-chart the top ten by set count.
Star Wars, City, Technic, and friends crowd the head — good sanity check that merges worked before you trust price scrapes.
Why scrape BrickEconomy? Rebrickable answers what exists; it does not answer what people pay on the secondary market. I used Playwright + asyncio to collect BrickEconomy pages — pydantic models for validation, aiohttp where fetch-only sufficed.
Scraper code, rate limits, and HTML drift handling: see LegosTracker repo — too long to paste here and keep maintainable.
Environment (reference) pip install playwright asyncio pydantic aiohttp pandas scikit-learn matplotlib playwright install Imports and async browser setup match the repo’s scraper/ module — run from project root with tests on a single set before batching thousands.
Price history for set 001-1 Classic 001-1 is a teaching anchor: long history, recognizable name, enough secondary-market churn to plot.
Pipeline:
Load scraped 001-1_history.csv / 001-1_new.csv from LegosTracker data folder. Clean dates and outliers (bad rows from HTML changes). Plot price vs time — look for step changes around reissues and collector spikes. Linear regression — humble forecast Fit a simple linear model on engineered features (time, condition flags, maybe part count proxies) to predict logged price.
It is not alpha — it is explainability practice:
Does trend dominate? Do residuals cluster by era? Would a tree model buy you much on N=small? Full coefficient tables and train/test split notes: Medium original article and repo notebooks.
Notebook excerpts The Medium import contained pages of one-line pandas plots. Prefer the GitHub project for copy-pasteable cells:
Theme merges and bar charts Scraper orchestration Price cleaning sklearn regression pipeline When not to trust this analysis Pitfall Effect Scraper breakage Missing months look like price crashes Survivorship in sets table Discontinued sets skew counts Linear model on hype sets Residuals explode Treating resale as MSRP Different economic story Takeaway LEGO data is messy fun — good for pandas practice, async scraping discipline, and remembering that secondary prices are sentiment plus plastic, not fundamentals.

I batch-ran EMA and MACD strategies across many tickers with BatchBacktesting — FMP for equities, Binance for crypto. This post explains what the runner does, how to read outrageous leaderboard rows, and why that is not a live trading system. Version française.
What BatchBacktesting is A Python project that:
Pulls OHLCV via Financial Modeling Prep (S&P list) or Binance (crypto list). Applies a strategy class (EMA or MACD) per ticker. Writes CSV + optional HTML charts under output/. It is a screening hammer, not a portfolio manager.
Install and run (sketch) pip install numpy httpx rich backtesting pandas_ta from batch_backtesting import run_backtests, EMA, MACD tickers = get_SP500() run_backtests(tickers, strategy=EMA, num_threads=12, generate_plots=True) run_backtests(get_all_crypto(), strategy=MACD, num_threads=12, generate_plots=True) Exact imports and API keys live in the GitHub README — do not commit keys.
Interpreting example leaderboard rows From an EMA batch (illustrative):
Ticker Return Gut check BTCBUSD +293% Crypto volatility + parameter fit BTTBUSD -99% Penny-style blow-up — liquidity not modeled UAL / NCLH deep negative COVID-era windows punish naive trend rules Top and bottom lists are diagnostics, not buy/sell lists. Always open the per-ticker chart (example AAPL chart) before storytelling.
What the Medium import left out on purpose The original article embedded long pasted code blocks for every helper — maintenance belongs in the repo, not this Hugo page. For:
HTTP helpers, threading, CSV writers → see BatchBacktesting source. Full French walkthrough → Medium canonical URL. When not to use this Misuse Why it hurts Deploy top row ticker live Overfit to window Ignore fees/slippage Backtest inflates Skip out-of-sample dates Regime change breaks rule Takeaway Batch runs teach distribution of outcomes under a dumb rule — invaluable for humility, dangerous as autopilot.
